page: UpCloud CLOUDNATIVE-4xCPU-48GB is a KVM-hypervised virtual server featuring 4 shared vCPUs mapped to 4 physical cores of an AMD EPYC 7542 processor running at 2.0 GHz. The x86_64 architecture includes 16 MB of L3 cache, 0.5 MB of L2 cache, and 64 KB of L1d cache per core. It is equipped with 48.0 GB of system memory, yielding a high memory-to-core ratio of 12.0 GB per core. This instance does not include local storage or dedicated GPU hardware, but it comes with one complimentary public IPv4 address.

Performance benchmarks reveal a mixed capability profile. The shared CPU allocation results in poor single-core stress-ng performance and weak multi-core stress-ng performance. However, Geekbench testing shows strong single-core performance and strong text processing capabilities, alongside average multi-core and software compilation scores. Memory bandwidth is average for cached small-block reads but drops to weak levels for large-block uncached reads and writes. Database operations, Redis SET operations, and static web serving throughput also fall into the bottom performance tier.

The primary tradeoff of this server is its high memory capacity paired with shared CPU resources, which limits its suitability for sustained, high-throughput compute workloads. From a qualitative cost-efficiency perspective, the instance offers a dense memory allocation relative to its virtual CPU count, making it a viable option for memory-intensive workloads that do not require continuous, dedicated CPU performance. Suitable workloads include text processing, cached memory operations, software compilation, and lightweight or development-stage database and web serving tasks where CPU resource sharing does not bottleneck operations.

Lacking local storage and dedicated GPU hardware, this instance provides a high memory-to-core ratio of 12.0 GB per core. Benchmark data indicates a performance tradeoff: while Geekbench single-core and text processing scores are strong, stress-ng CPU performance, large-block memory bandwidth, and Redis SET operations fall into the lower percentiles due to the shared CPU allocation. It is best suited for memory-heavy, low-CPU-intensity workloads such as text processing, software compilation, and development environments.
